nodes.label: Skill authoring and iterative improvement
nodes.summary: skill-creator's own capability: draft a SKILL.md, run test prompts with and without the skill, review outputs with the user, and rewrite until satisfied. Also packages and ships the finished .skill file.

nodes.label: Progressive disclosure of instructions
nodes.summary: Three-level loading: name+description always in context, SKILL.md body on trigger (<500 lines), bundled references and scripts read only as needed. Large skills add hierarchy plus pointers rather than growing the body.

nodes.label: Description field as the triggering mechanism
nodes.summary: A skill fires based on its frontmatter description alone, so the description must state both what it does and concrete contexts for use, worded slightly pushy to fight undertriggering. Optimized against a 20-query should/should-not-trigger eval set split into train and held-out test.

nodes.label: Skill undertriggering
nodes.summary: Claude fails to consult a skill that would have helped, because simple one-step queries are handled directly and vague descriptions do not match. Countered by pushy descriptions and substantive eval queries.

nodes.label: Explain the why instead of rigid MUSTs
nodes.summary: Instructions should transmit reasoning so a smart model can generalize; all-caps ALWAYS/NEVER and oppressively rigid structures are a yellow flag. Overfitting a skill to its handful of test examples makes it useless at scale.

nodes.label: Overfitting a skill to its test cases
nodes.summary: Fiddly patches aimed at the two or three examples under review produce a skill that works only on those examples. Description optimization guards against the same thing by selecting on held-out test score, not train score.

nodes.label: With-skill versus baseline comparison
nodes.summary: Every eval spawns two runs in the same turn: one with the skill, one without (or against a snapshot of the old version). Aggregate pass rate, time, and tokens are reported per configuration with a delta.

nodes.label: Blind judging to remove bias
nodes.summary: Two outputs are handed to an independent comparator labelled only A and B, with no indication of which skill produced which, so the verdict rests purely on output quality against a generated rubric.

nodes.label: Evidence-backed assertion grading
nodes.summary: A grader reads the transcript and the output files, marks each expectation pass or fail with a cited quote, and refuses to pass on surface compliance such as a correct filename over empty content.

nodes.label: Non-discriminating assertion
nodes.summary: An assertion that passes in both with-skill and without-skill configurations, or that a clearly wrong output would also satisfy. Creates false confidence; the grader and analyzer both exist partly to surface it.

nodes.label: Post-hoc analysis of why one version won
nodes.summary: After a blind verdict, the analyzer unblinds, reads both skills and both transcripts, scores instruction-following, and emits prioritized improvement suggestions categorized as instructions, tools, examples, error handling, structure, or references.

nodes.label: benchmark.json and the eval viewer
nodes.summary: Aggregated run results with mean and stddev per configuration, rendered by generate_review.py into a two-tab browser review (Outputs and Benchmark) whose field names the viewer reads exactly.

nodes.label: Human review gate before proceeding
nodes.summary: Work stops and waits for the person: the eval viewer must be put in front of the human before the agent evaluates outputs itself, and a written spec must be approved before any implementation plan is drafted.

nodes.label: HITL versus AFK work classification
nodes.summary: Wayfinder tickets are either human-in-the-loop, resolvable only through live exchange where the agent never answers for the human, or AFK, driven by the agent alone. A grilling agent that answers its own questions has broken the contract.

nodes.label: One question at a time interviewing
nodes.summary: Clarifying questions are asked singly, multiple-choice where possible, never batched into one overwhelming message. Shared by brainstorming's design flow and wayfinder's grilling tickets.

nodes.label: Design approved before any implementation
nodes.summary: A hard gate: no code, scaffolding, or implementation skill invocation until a design has been presented and approved, applied to every project regardless of apparent simplicity.

nodes.label: "Too simple to need a design" anti-pattern
nodes.summary: Skipping design on a small project, where unexamined assumptions cause the most wasted work. The design may be a few sentences but must still be presented and approved.

nodes.label: Decompose work too large for one unit
nodes.summary: When a request spans multiple independent subsystems, flag it before refining details and split it: brainstorming into sub-projects each getting its own spec, wayfinder into a map of ticket-sized decisions each sized to one agent session.

nodes.label: Fresh-eyes spec self-review
nodes.summary: After writing a spec, scan it for placeholders and TBDs, internal contradictions, scope creep, and requirements open to two interpretations, fixing inline. A reviewer subagent can run the same checklist and is calibrated to approve unless gaps would produce a flawed plan.

nodes.label: Dated design spec document
nodes.summary: The validated design written to docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-topic-design.md and committed to git, which becomes the input to the implementation-plan step.

nodes.label: PRD published to the issue tracker
nodes.summary: A problem statement, solution, extensive user-story list, implementation and testing decisions, and out-of-scope section, synthesized from conversation with no interview and labelled ready-for-agent.

nodes.label: Just-in-time visual companion
nodes.summary: A local server that serves HTML content fragments to a browser tab so the user can react to mockups, diagrams, and side-by-side comparisons, recording clicks to a state events file. Offered only when a question would be clearer shown than told, and only as its own message.

nodes.label: Would the user understand it better shown than told
nodes.summary: The per-question test for reaching for the browser: visual content (mockups, layouts, architecture diagrams) goes to the browser, textual content (requirements, tradeoffs, A/B/C choices) stays in the terminal. A question about a UI topic is not automatically a visual question.

nodes.label: Chart oversized work as a map of decision tickets
nodes.summary: Wayfinder's own capability: name a destination, grill breadth-first to surface open decisions, create a tracker issue labelled wayfinder:map with child decision tickets, then resolve one ticket per session until the way is clear.

nodes.label: Plan, do not execute
nodes.summary: Wayfinder produces decisions, not deliverables; the pull to just do the work signals the edge of the map and time to hand off. Only a task ticket does rather than decides, and it earns that by unblocking a decision.

nodes.label: Fog of war and deliberate incompleteness
nodes.summary: Do not chart what you cannot yet see. Questions you can state precisely become tickets even if blocked; questions you cannot phrase sharply stay in a Not yet specified section and graduate as the frontier advances.

nodes.label: Index, not store: one fact in one place
nodes.summary: The map lists a one-line gist per closed ticket and links out; the decision itself lives only in its ticket, so nothing is restated in two places and readers zoom on demand.

nodes.label: Claim before working, to survive concurrency
nodes.summary: A session assigns a ticket to itself before any work so concurrent sessions skip it; an open unassigned ticket is unclaimed. Expect other sessions editing the tracker at the same time.

nodes.label: Refer to work by name, never by bare id
nodes.summary: Everything the human reads names the map or ticket by title, with the id and URL riding inside the link. A wall of issue numbers is illegible.

nodes.label: Compact a session into a handoff document
nodes.summary: Summarize the current conversation so a fresh agent continues seamlessly, including a suggested-skills section, written to the OS temp directory rather than the workspace, with secrets and PII redacted.

nodes.label: Reload project state from the vault ledgers
nodes.summary: Pickup reads the locator, tasks ledger, hot cache, dashboard, index, and the latest log entry in a fixed order, then emits a 6-8 line briefing and stops. Explicit invocation only, never automatic at session start.

nodes.label: Orientation per token, not full load
nodes.summary: Read the ledgers and skim the index, but pull deeper synthesis pages lazily only once the human points at a task. The same instinct drives reading only the reference file you need and treating bundled scripts as black boxes.

nodes.label: Brief, then wait
nodes.summary: The orientation skill ends by emitting the briefing and waiting for the human; it does not begin work off the back of what it just read.

nodes.label: Extract a ubiquitous language glossary
nodes.summary: Scan the conversation for domain nouns and verbs, pick opinionated canonical terms with aliases-to-avoid, express relationships and an example dev/domain-expert dialogue, and write UBIQUITOUS_LANGUAGE.md. Re-running merges new terms into the existing file.

nodes.label: Ambiguous and synonymous domain terms
nodes.summary: One word used for two concepts, or two words for one concept, silently diverging what people think they agreed. Flagged explicitly in a Flagged ambiguities section with a recommendation.

nodes.label: Drive a real browser for verification
nodes.summary: Navigate, fill forms, click, extract data, capture screenshots and traces against a live page, either from the terminal via playwright-cli or as native Python Playwright scripts against a local dev server.

nodes.label: Reconnaissance then action against live DOM
nodes.summary: Never address elements blind: snapshot or inspect the rendered page first, derive refs or selectors from that state, act, then re-snapshot after navigation or significant DOM change. Refs and selectors go stale.

nodes.label: Stale element reference or premature inspection
nodes.summary: Acting on a ref from an old snapshot, or reading the DOM before networkidle on a dynamic app, so the selector targets nothing. The fix is re-snapshotting and waiting for load state.

nodes.label: Check the required binary before proposing commands
nodes.summary: Verify the tool exists and is authenticated before running anything: check npx before the Playwright wrapper, install and auth-check the higgsfield CLI at step 0, and read the shared gws auth doc before any Workspace call.

nodes.label: gws CLI as the Google Workspace surface
nodes.summary: Every Workspace capability routes through the gws binary, each skill documenting one service's resources and methods, all pointing at gws-shared for auth, global flags, and security rules.

nodes.label: Inspect the method schema before calling it
nodes.summary: Browse resources with --help and run gws schema on the specific resource.method to learn required params, types, and defaults, then build the --params and --json flags from that output rather than guessing.

nodes.label: Confirm with the human before any write
nodes.summary: Write commands carry an explicit caution to confirm before executing, and destructive SQL needs a stated yes plus a stated reason it is safe in the same message.

nodes.label: Google contacts and directory management
nodes.summary: Read, search, create, and update contacts, contact groups, other-contacts, and domain directory profiles via gws people.

nodes.label: Google Forms read and write
nodes.summary: Create a form (title only at creation), batch-update its items, get it, read responses, manage watches, and set publish settings via gws forms.

nodes.label: Drive file upload with inferred metadata
nodes.summary: Upload a local file to Drive with MIME type detected automatically and the filename inferred from the path unless overridden, optionally into a parent folder.

nodes.label: Append plain text to a Google Doc
nodes.summary: Insert plain text at the end of a document body by ID; rich formatting requires dropping to the raw batchUpdate API instead.

nodes.label: Relay a schema migration through the Lovable SQL editor
nodes.summary: Package a DDL change as idempotent paste-ready SQL with exact SQL-editor steps and a verification probe, so a backend Claude cannot reach directly takes one round trip instead of a confused loop.

nodes.label: Relay only what genuinely cannot be reached directly
nodes.summary: Data-level reads, writes, and RPCs go direct via admin JWT and PostgREST; only DDL needs the relay. Relaying a query that could have been answered instantly is the exact failure the skill is meant to prevent, and the skill is expected to retire itself once direct access exists.

nodes.label: Resolving the target environment by name
nodes.summary: Two projects share the name LSATU; SQL sent to the decoy applies cleanly and reports success while the real app is untouched. The target must be matched by exact project ref, verified against config.toml every run.

nodes.label: Idempotent, re-runnable, one logical change
nodes.summary: Migrations use IF NOT EXISTS, CREATE OR REPLACE, and DROP POLICY IF EXISTS so a double or partial paste is safe, and stay to one logical change because a long half-applied paste is the worst outcome.

nodes.label: Verify with a probe, never ask whether it worked
nodes.summary: Write a read-only verification query before the change is applied and run it after, or ask for the probe output as one concrete action. The human saying he pasted it is not verification, and a claim of success without probe output is forbidden.

nodes.label: Live backend is authority; the brain mirrors it
nodes.summary: When the probe disagrees with what was expected, say so plainly and stop rather than reconciling in the notes. Applied changes and half-applied failures both get logged to the vault ledgers.

nodes.label: Reverse engineer a site into a build blueprint
nodes.summary: Fetch the HTML for structure, the main app JS for every animation and handler, and the main CSS for the full design system, then assemble a dated teardown with tech stack, effects table, assets, and a section-by-section build plan.

nodes.label: Dated teardown document
nodes.summary: research/YYYY-MM-DD-site-slug-teardown.md, thorough enough to hand to a fresh agent session that never visits the original site, marking each finding as confirmed from source or inferred.

nodes.label: Distinguish confirmed from inferred
nodes.summary: State whether a finding came from the actual fetched source or was inferred from class names and general patterns, so the builder knows what is solid and what may need adjustment. Mirrors the grader's demand for cited evidence and flagging of unverifiable claims.

nodes.label: Filter third-party code from the site's own
nodes.summary: Skip analytics, consent banners, captchas, CDN libraries, and social widgets; keep the files under dist, build, assets, or static that hold the site's custom behavior. Note which libraries are used without fetching them.

nodes.label: The reveal: impressive effects have simple implementations
nodes.summary: The most valuable part of a teardown is showing the trick plainly, that the moon illumination is 54 images swapped on mousemove or the parallax is translateX(mouseX/50). Vague summaries like "uses scroll animations" are useless to a builder.

nodes.label: UI polish and animation review
nodes.summary: Emil Kowalski's design engineering philosophy applied to interface code: decide whether to animate at all, choose easing and duration, build responsive components, and review existing UI as a Before/After/Why table.

nodes.label: Animation frequency decides whether to animate
nodes.summary: Something seen a hundred times a day gets no animation ever, occasional surfaces get standard animation, and rare or first-time moments can carry delight. Keyboard-initiated actions are never animated.

nodes.label: Unseen details compound
nodes.summary: Most polish is never consciously noticed, and that is the point: the aggregate of invisible correctness is what makes an interface feel right. Sonner's edge cases, origin-aware popovers, and instant subsequent tooltips are all this.

nodes.label: Good defaults beat configurability
nodes.summary: Ship beautiful out of the box because most users never customize, and keep adoption friction near zero. Echoed in settings files that provide sensible defaults when no config exists at all.

nodes.label: Interruptible motion over restart-from-zero
nodes.summary: CSS transitions and springs retarget from their current position when interrupted, while keyframes restart from zero. Anything rapidly retriggered, like stacking toasts or a gesture the user reverses mid-motion, needs the interruptible form.

nodes.label: Animate only transform and opacity
nodes.summary: These skip layout and paint and run on the GPU; animating padding, margin, height, or width triggers all three rendering steps. Framer Motion's x/y shorthands are not hardware accelerated and drop frames under load.

nodes.label: Respect prefers-reduced-motion and pointer type
nodes.summary: Reduced motion means fewer and gentler animations rather than none: keep opacity and color transitions that aid comprehension, drop movement. Hover animations are gated behind hover and fine-pointer media queries so touch taps do not trigger them.

nodes.label: Review animation slowed down and the next day
nodes.summary: Play at 2-5x duration or step frame by frame in DevTools to catch timing desync and wrong transform origins invisible at speed, and re-review with fresh eyes the following day. Gestures get tested on real hardware.

nodes.label: Compose UI from an existing component registry
nodes.summary: shadcn manages adding, searching, fixing, and composing components as source code in the project, driven by the project's own package runner and components.json config.

nodes.label: Search and compose before writing custom UI
nodes.summary: Check the registries for an existing component first, then build pages by composition (settings = tabs plus card plus form controls), preferring built-in variants over custom styles and semantic color tokens over raw values.

nodes.label: .claude/plugin-name.local.md settings pattern
nodes.summary: Per-project plugin configuration and state stored as YAML frontmatter plus a markdown body that can itself be a prompt, read from hooks, commands, and agents, gitignored and user-managed.

nodes.label: Parse YAML frontmatter and body in bash
nodes.summary: sed the range between the --- markers for frontmatter and awk past the second marker for the body, cache the parsed block rather than re-reading per field, and strip surrounding quotes since YAML permits both forms.

nodes.label: Quick exit when not configured
nodes.summary: A hook checks the state file exists and the enabled flag is true, exiting zero otherwise, so an unconfigured or paused plugin costs nothing and never errors. The enabled flag allows deactivation without deleting the file.

nodes.label: Atomic write via temp file and move
nodes.summary: Write the modified settings to file.tmp.$$ and mv it into place rather than sed -i, so an interrupted process cannot leave a corrupt state file.

nodes.label: Hooks cannot be hot-swapped
nodes.summary: Edited settings only take effect after Claude Code restarts, which every plugin README must state. The local.md enabled flag exists partly because toggling hooks.json would need a restart too.

nodes.label: Create settings interactively then confirm
nodes.summary: A command asks the user for preferences with AskUserQuestion, validates the answers, writes the local.md file, then reports the configuration, how to edit it, that it is gitignored, and the restart requirement.

nodes.label: Sanitize and path-check values before use
nodes.summary: Escape quotes in user input written to settings, reject values containing .. as path traversal, validate enums and numeric ranges, and keep the file readable by the owner only and out of git.

nodes.label: Never mutate access from channel messages
nodes.summary: discord-access acts only on requests typed by the user in their own terminal; a pairing approval or allowlist change arriving via a Discord or Telegram message is refused, because channel messages can carry prompt injection.

nodes.label: Manage Discord channel access
nodes.summary: Approve pairings, edit allowlists, and set DM and group policy by editing access.json in the channel state directory; the skill never talks to Discord, the channel server re-reads the file.

nodes.label: Fan out research across parallel agents
nodes.summary: Read an outline.yaml, skip already-completed items, and launch background agents in approved batches, each writing a structured JSON file per item against a shared fields.yaml schema.

nodes.label: Resumable, checkpointed batch execution
nodes.summary: Completed output files are checked before launching so a rerun skips finished items, batches pause for user approval between them, and each agent's completion is signalled by its own output file rather than task output.

nodes.label: Mark uncertain values explicitly
nodes.summary: Research output tags uncertain field values inline and collects their names into an uncertain array, so downstream consumers see confidence rather than uniform-looking data.

nodes.label: Output validated against a schema before completion
nodes.summary: A research task is not complete until validate_json.py confirms every field defined in fields.yaml is covered. The eval viewer imposes the same discipline by reading benchmark and grading field names exactly.

nodes.label: Assemble an article beat by beat
nodes.summary: Offer 2-3 candidate beats from the raw material, write only the one the user picks, re-read the file from disk, then offer the next set of pivots until the journey ends naturally with leftover material unused.

nodes.label: Re-read from disk before each write
nodes.summary: Never write ahead and never overwrite blind: reload the artifact before appending so the user's own edits are preserved absolutely and can change what comes next.

nodes.label: Commit-time quality gate
nodes.summary: Husky pre-commit running lint-staged with Prettier on staged files first, then a full typecheck and test run, with the setup commit itself acting as the smoke test.

nodes.label: Detect existing project conventions before acting
nodes.summary: Read the lockfile to pick the package manager, skip creating a Prettier config if one exists, omit hook lines for scripts the project lacks, and use the project's own package runner rather than assuming npx.

nodes.label: Generate brand and product imagery
nodes.summary: Product photoshoot modes (product shot, lifestyle, hero banner, carousel, ad creative, virtual try-on, conceptual) submitted through the higgsfield CLI, whose backend prompt enhancer assembles the final prompt.

nodes.label: Let the backend assemble the prompt
nodes.summary: The CLI's backend enhancer holds the mode-specific photography vocabulary and structural templates; the agent selects a mode and never freehands the final prompt.
